lessons.title: Software development life cycle and testing
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board — Advanced Level Computer Science syllabus (Upper Sixth part) — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the stages of the life cycle
Compare waterfall, prototyping and agile approaches
Design a test plan with normal, boundary and erroneous data
Distinguish types of testing and maintenance
reviewNotes: SDLC stage names vary between textbooks; the Board's list of models should be checked.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Life cycle stages
blocks.md: **Analysis** (find and record requirements, feasibility study), **design** (structure, data, interface, algorithms), **implementation** (coding), **testing**, **deployment** (installation, training), **maintenance** (corrective, adaptive, perfective). Documentation (user and technical) is produced along the way.

blocks.title: Development models
blocks.md: **Waterfall**: stages in strict sequence; clear and well documented but inflexible if requirements change. **Prototyping**: build a quick working model, get user feedback and refine; good when requirements are unclear. **Agile**: short **iterations** (sprints), working software each time, close contact with the customer, accepts changing requirements; less documentation.

blocks.caption: Five stages from analysis to maintenance, each leading to the next.
blocks.alt: Vertical flow of the waterfall stages: analysis, design, implementation, testing, maintenance.

blocks.title: Testing
blocks.md: A **test plan** lists the test, the input data, the expected result and the actual result. Use **normal** data (valid), **boundary** data (at the limits of the valid range) and **erroneous** data (invalid). Example: marks must be 0-100: normal 55, boundary 0 and 100 (and 101 or -1 just outside), erroneous 'abc'. Types: **unit**, **integration**, **system**, **acceptance** (by the user), **alpha/beta**; **black-box** (inputs and outputs only) and **white-box** (internal logic).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Testing only normal data.
- Writing the 'expected result' after seeing the program's output.
- Choosing a model by habit: the right model depends on how clear and stable the requirements are.
- Maintenance is part of the life cycle, not a sign of failure.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Test data
blocks.statement: A program accepts a mark from 0 to 100. Choose normal, boundary and erroneous test data.
steps: Normal: 55. Boundary: 0 and 100 (and just outside: -1 and 101 should be rejected).
Erroneous: abc (text) or an empty entry; expected result: an error message.

blocks.title: Example 2 - Choose a model
blocks.statement: A clinic in Bamenda wants an appointment system but is not sure what it needs. Which approach is suitable?
steps: Requirements are unclear and will change after users see something.
Prototyping or agile development with frequent feedback suits this.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Compare the waterfall and agile approaches for developing a school management system.
exercises.model: Waterfall: fixed requirements, stages in order, well documented, difficult to change later. Agile: short iterations with working software and user feedback, handles changing requirements, less documentation. For a school, if requirements are unclear or likely to change, agile is more suitable; if fixed and well understood, waterfall can work.
exercises.rubric: 1 mark each for a correct point on waterfall, agile, a comparison, and a justified recommendation (4 marks).
